# The Water in Your Glass

Right now there is probably a glass of water within reach of you, or a kettle somewhere in your house, or a puddle you walked past this morning. Whatever water it is, it has been around far longer than any of us. It has been a cloud, a glacier, a river, the sweat of an animal, and the inside of a fern. Water doesn't get used up. It just keeps moving through the same loop, evaporating, falling, soaking into soil, and rising again.

Some of the molecules in your glass may have been in the lungs of a dinosaur, or in the tears of someone who lived in the Middle Ages. This sounds like a poetic exaggeration, but it's just arithmetic. The volume of water on Earth is roughly constant, and it mixes thoroughly over geological time. A single water molecule might spend a few thousand years in the deep ocean, a few hundred in a glacier, and a few days in the atmosphere before it rains on a field somewhere. Over a long enough span, every molecule visits everywhere.

I find this steadying. We tend to think of things as belonging to a particular moment: this cup, this year, this version of ourselves. But the matter we're made of is on loan. The carbon in your cells was forged in stars. The calcium in your bones was once part of some ancient reef. The iron in your blood was made in the death throes of a star that exploded before the Sun existed. We are temporary arrangements of very old material, briefly organized into something that can notice itself.

There is something almost unbearably generous in that. The universe doesn't keep score. It recycles. Nothing is wasted, though nothing is kept, either. The water that refreshed a child's hands in a river last spring might be part of a thunderhead over the ocean next week, and then part of a snowfield in a range you'll never visit.

I don't think this should make us feel small. Instead it suggests a kind of kinship with everything else. Your glass of water connects you, in a literal chemical way, to the rain forests, the polar caps, the mammoths, and the strangers on the other side of the planet who are drinking from the same circulating supply.

So the next time you pour a glass, consider drinking it slowly. You're taking in something that has been everywhere, and that is about to become a part of you, and then, eventually, a part of everything else again.
